newsitem.title: FRANCE: Car bomb kills one, wounds 10 in Algiers hotel.
newsitem.headline: Car bomb kills one, wounds 10 in Algiers hotel.

text.p: A car bomb exploded on Tuesday in front of a hotel in central Algiers, killing one person and wounding 10, Algerian security forces said in a statement read on Algerian state-run radio.

Witnesses, speaking by telephone from Algiers, said the bomb went off at about 5.45 a.m. (0445 GMT), by the Hotel Angleterre in downtown Algiers, badly damaging the hotel. They said they saw several people at the scene who had been wounded.

"The explosion has destroyed the front of the four-storey hotel. All its windows were blown out by the blast and shattered glass was strewn everywhere," said a telecommunications employee who saw the hotel.
Residents said security forces had ringed the area.

One Algiers resident said he has heard the blast from his house located in a suburb four km (2.5 miles) away. Witnesses said the powerful blast also shattered windows in several buildings up to 300 metres (yards) away.

It was the third bomb explosion in the last 10 days. No one claimed responsibility but residents said the explosion carried the hallmark of Moslem militants, blamed by the authorities for a series of bombings in which several hundred civilians have been killed in the past two years.
The main legal Moslem fundamentalist Hamas party said on Tuesday the continuing killings conflicted with government statements over an improvement in the security situation.

Hamas said in a statement that a party official named Zayed Rabah was killed in a bomb blast last Friday in the coastal town of Staoueli, near Algiers, and a second party official was killed by an armed gang last Friday in Ain Defla province, 115 km (70 miles) southwest of Algiers.
"While some officials reassert that 'we defeated terrorism', violence is still hitting innocent citizens, their lives and their property in some regions of the country," it added.
Hamas, which has a junior minister in the Algerian government, is at loggerheads with radical Islamists staging a four-year-old guerrilla war to try to topple the North African government.

An estimated 50,000 people have died in violence pitting Moslem rebels against government forces since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a commanding lead.
